title: Development redistributes working time across age and gender through schooling, pensions, social spending, and regulation
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11473, Global Working Hours
geography: 160 countries covering 97% of the world population in cross section, with time series spanning more than 20 years in 86 countries

observations.period: Global hours worked database; cross section of 160 countries

denominator.unit: countries in the cross-sectional labor-force-survey microdatabase

population_coverage.value: the database covers 97% of the world population in cross section

survey_scale.value: about 470 million individuals are represented in the harmonized survey microdata

global_gender_hours.value: women supply 35% of GDP-producing hours and men 65%; women’s average hours are 55% of men’s
global_gender_hours.unit: share and ratio of GDP-producing hours

time_as_resource.value: working time is a social distributional resource shaped by employment rates and hours per worker, not only an individual labor-supply choice

observations.method: Harmonized labor-force-survey microdatabase combining hours, employment, age, gender, schooling, and related socioeconomic variables.
observations.uncertainty: Survey definitions differ across countries; actual versus usual hours, main-job versus all-job measures, seasonality, unpaid household work, and agricultural coverage limit exact comparability.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, young people, prime-age adults, older adults, employed and non-employed people, unpaid caregivers, and households organized around paid work and care.
observations.counterinterpretation: GDP-producing hours exclude unpaid cooking, cleaning, childcare, and eldercare, so the database does not measure total socially necessary work or overall time well-being.

observations.period: Cross-country development comparisons by age and gender

denominator.unit: age groups used in the paper: young 15-19, prime-age 20-59, elderly 60+

overall_development.value: hours worked per adult decline only slightly with GDP per capita and are weakly correlated with development overall

young_and_elderly.value: hours worked by ages 15-19 and 60+ decline with development, with the cross-country reductions explained entirely by rising school attendance and public pension coverage

prime_age.value: prime-age hours worked are stable or slightly increasing with GDP per adult

gender_reshuffling.value: falling male hours per worker are quantitatively offset by rising female labor-force participation in many countries

social_meaning.value: development changes who works, when, and under which institutions rather than simply reducing the total amount of work

observations.method: Cross-country regressions and country time-series analysis of hours per adult, hours per worker, employment rates, age, gender, GDP per adult, school attendance, and pension coverage.
observations.uncertainty: The paper reports associations and explanatory correlations, not causal estimates of schooling, pensions, development, or gender norms; within-country time-series patterns differ from cross-country relationships.
observations.subgroup: Adolescents balancing school and work, older adults with or without pensions, prime-age women and men, households with different care arrangements, and workers in countries with different social norms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower youth or elderly paid work may indicate improved protection, but it may also reflect exclusion, weak labor demand, health constraints, or unmeasured unpaid work; higher female participation does not imply equal job quality or autonomy.

observations.period: Prime-age hours and public policy indicators across countries

denominator.unit: policy domains examined: labor taxes, social spending, and working-time regulations

labor_taxes.value: labor income taxes are strongly negatively related to hours worked across countries

social_spending.value: the labor-tax relationship is attenuated after controlling for social spending

working_time_regulation.value: the labor-tax relationship disappears after further controlling for working-hours regulations; both social spending and regulations are associated with lower hours worked

policy_tradeoff.value: the observed association is consistent with taxes financing transfers and institutions that reduce hours, rather than a simple tax-only work disincentive

consumer_household_route.value: time policy can alter household room for care, consumption, rest, and civic participation, but these outcomes are not measured directly

observations.method: Exploratory cross-country regressions relating prime-age hours to net-of-tax labor income, social spending, transfers, formal employment, and an index of working-time regulations.
observations.uncertainty: Policy variables are endogenous and jointly determined with development, labor-market structure, norms, and institutions; correlations cannot rank policy interventions or establish a causal hours response.
observations.subgroup: Formal and informal workers, parents and caregivers, low- and high-income households, women and men, employers, unions, and governments designing tax and social-protection systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shorter paid hours may reflect healthier work standards and social protection, but can also coexist with low incomes, multiple jobs, unpaid care burdens, or involuntary underemployment.

boundary: This record adds a development-to-time-allocation mechanism. It measures paid or GDP-producing work through labor-force surveys and does not measure unpaid care, rest, subjective time pressure, job quality, household consumption, bargaining power, or causal policy effects. The gender, age, cultural, consumer, and political implications are hypotheses for follow-through, not direct outcomes established by this cross-country evidence.
